title: Ukraine Fires 1,015 Drones at Russia as Trump Attacks the Strikes, Taipei Repels 16 Chinese Vessels, and France Counts 2,400 Arrests
subhead: Ukraine's largest drone campaign of the war hit St Petersburg's oil terminal and closed its airport overnight; Washington responded by attacking Kyiv rather than Moscow. Taiwan's coast guard pushed back a coordinated Chinese flotilla near Dongsha, and Macron addressed the nation after riots gutted a city hall in Limoges.

sections.heading: Kyiv Sends 1,015 Drones Into Russia Overnight
sections.body:
Russia's Defence Ministry said it neutralised 1,015 Ukrainian drones overnight across 15 regions, Crimea and the Black Sea, Al Jazeera reports — one of Kyiv's largest aerial operations of the war. St Petersburg Governor Alexander Beglov said fires broke out at the St Petersburg oil terminal, the Ruchi oil depot and warehouses in the Kolpinsky district. At least one person was killed and five injured, residential buildings were hit, and the city's main airport restricted operations for safety. Leningrad Governor Alexander Drozdenko said 145 drones were shot down over his region and about 20,000 people lost electricity. In the city itself, e-commerce firm Ozon reported a fire at a logistics hub and VK said drones struck its data centre in the wider region, with services unaffected.

The timing is the story. The strike landed the same weekend Trump publicly defended his Friday decision to suspend new Russia sanctions for 60 days, saying he did not want to 'foolishly' drive Moscow away from the negotiating table. In the same social-media post he blamed Zelenskyy for the refinery and depot strikes, claiming the Ukrainian president 'doesn't want to end this war'. The 'energy ceasefire' Trump announced on October 11 had already collapsed; Zelenskyy told the Financial Times he was done with it after Moscow kept hitting Ukraine's grid. Zelenskyy wrote on X on Sunday that Russia had again attacked Ukrainian energy, oil and other infrastructure, and said the war 'must be brought to an end'. Al Jazeera describes communication between Washington and Kyiv as 'virtually nonstop' — but the direction of pressure is now unmistakable.

The operational logic cuts against Washington's preference. Ukrainian strikes since March have degraded Russian refining and logistics, and Kyiv has no other comparable lever over Moscow's war economy. A US administration that restrains those strikes while also pausing sanctions has effectively removed both of its own pressure instruments in the same week — one at Ukraine's request and one against it.
sections.whyItMatters: The US is now simultaneously blocking new sanctions and criticising the only coercive tool Kyiv still has. Watch whether Congress moves to override the 60-day waiver or whether allied refinery supplies to Ukraine become the substitute.

sections.heading: Taipei Drives Off 16 Chinese Vessels in a Coordinated Sweep
sections.body:
Taiwan's coast guard said on Sunday it confronted and drove away 16 Chinese coast guard, research and fishing vessels taking part in what it called simultaneous 'maritime harassment' operations around Taiwan's main island and Pratas (Dongsha), the disputed island to the southwest, Al Jazeera reports. Taipei called the number of vessels 'unusually large', said four of them were fishing boats, some entered restricted waters, and described the pattern as 'hybrid warfare' intended to give a 'false impression of jurisdiction' and 'unilaterally alter the status quo'.

The numbers behind the incident are what matter. Taiwanese official data show Beijing deployed a record 244 coast guard, research and other ships around the main island in July, up from 58 in the same month the previous year, according to Al Jazeera. In a separate incident on October 1, Taiwan's coast guard fired water cannon at a Chinese fishing vessel near Pratas.

This is pressure applied below the threshold of military action: civilian-hulled vessels, nominally non-military agencies, and a legal claim that Beijing asserts and Taipei rejects. Last week the Liaoning carrier group transited the Ryukyus; this week the work is being done by coast guard cutters and fishing boats. The two tracks run in parallel — military signalling and administrative encroachment — which is precisely what makes the pattern difficult to answer without escalating.
sections.whyItMatters: Beijing is normalising jurisdiction-by-presence around Taiwan and Dongsha without firing a shot. Every encounter that Taipei resolves with water cannon and eviction establishes the operating procedure for the next, larger one.

sections.heading: France's Cost-of-Living Revolt Turns Into the Worst Disorder in Decades
sections.body:
Some 550,000 demonstrators marched across France on Saturday over fuel prices, the cost of living and deteriorating public services including schools. Groups in black, masked and wearing balaclavas, then rioted and looted in Paris, Marseille, Lille, Lyon and other cities, setting fire to cars and buildings, BBC reports. Police have arrested about 2,400 people, per the interior ministry. In Limoges, rioters burned the 19th-century city hall; its clock tower and roof collapsed.

Macron addressed the nation from the Élysée on Sunday, calling for 'calm and order', drawing a distinction between protesters' 'legitimate demands' and those who 'destroyed, smashed and looted', saying nothing justifies the violence, and warning against escalation. Looting and clashes continued on a smaller scale in Paris and Lyon on Sunday, with tear gas and stun grenades fired at hundreds of people according to AFP. Macron said local prefects and mayors would draft measures to protect shops and civic buildings and promised 'full transparency' over the police response.

Al Jazeera reports some 1,800 arrests and hundreds of injuries during the nationwide demonstrations — a figure that conflicts with the interior ministry's count via the BBC; the discrepancy likely reflects timing rather than substance, but the scale is not in dispute. For a government already stretched by Ukraine financing and EU budget fights, a domestic legitimacy crisis in its second-largest economy lands at the worst possible moment. The UK is not immune either: a similar cost-of-living protest wave has been building across Europe, and Albania has now seen six consecutive days of violent unrest in Tirana.
sections.whyItMatters: Macron's room to sell defence spending, Ukraine aid and EU fiscal reform to voters shrinks with every torched building. French political weakness directly weakens the EU's ability to act on Ukraine and trade.

sections.heading: EU Steel Tariffs Hit Kyiv While It Is Still Fighting
sections.body:
Yuriy Ryzhenkov, chief executive of Metinvest, one of Ukraine's largest steel producers, told the BBC that the EU's new steel import restrictions are 'unfair' and that Ukraine has been 'bundled together' with measures aimed at curbing cheap Chinese and Turkish imports. The EU has capped tax-free steel imports at 18.3 million tonnes a year — a 47% cut from 2024 levels — with country-specific quotas, but the Ukrainian industry estimates its exports to the EU could fall by 50–60%. A European Commission spokesperson told the BBC that Brussels 'took into account the difficult situation' of Ukraine and that Kyiv has a specific quota, while acknowledging it sits at a 'level lower than in the past years'. The EU–Ukraine free trade agreement does not shield Ukraine from separate trade defence measures.

Ryzhenkov's argument is blunt: 'Access to the European market is crucial for survival.' That is not rhetoric — steel is one of Ukraine's few remaining hard-currency export earners and a direct input into wartime revenue.

This is a small story with a large signal. Brussels is protecting domestic steelmakers from Chinese overcapacity, and Kyiv is caught as collateral. It follows last week's walkout by Western finance chiefs on Russia's minister at the IMF meetings in Bangkok, and it tells the same story: allied economic solidarity with Ukraine is being eroded one sector at a time by domestic protectionism.
sections.whyItMatters: Ukraine's war finance depends on exports that EU trade policy is now restricting. If Kyiv loses half its steel access, the funding gap has to be filled by grants — which are getting harder to sell in Paris, Berlin and Rome.

sections.heading: Sanaa Flares Again as Tehran Pins the War on Netanyahu
sections.body:
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi accused Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of pushing for more conflict and 'driving America into another war to stay out of jail', Al Jazeera's Iran war live blog reports. Trump said Russia is 'doing very little, if anything' to help Iran in the ongoing war. Fighting in Yemen flared again, with the live blog citing a Sanaa street scene as the visual for the day's coverage.

The Yemen theatre remains the most consequential for the Gulf: the October 11 attack that killed 12 at Riyadh's airport and the Sisi government's move last week to authorise defence assistance to Saudi Arabia both follow from it. Egypt's parliament authorised Sisi on Saturday to approve any Saudi request for assistance, which would put Egyptian forces — however defined — into the Saudi air-defence picture for the first time.

The rhetorical shift worth noting is where Tehran is directing blame. Framing the war as Netanyahu's personal project, rather than Israel's, leaves room for a US–Iran channel even while fighting continues — and Trump's jab at Russian non-help reinforces that read. Whether that opening is real or rhetorical is the open question.
sections.whyItMatters: Iran is trying to separate Washington from Jerusalem rhetorically while Egypt moves closer to Saudi defence. The Gulf's air-defence burden is being redistributed in real time.

sections.heading: Gaza's Crossings Shut for a Fifth Day and a Venezuelan Opposition Reset
sections.body:
Israeli restrictions on commercial goods entering Gaza entered a fifth consecutive day, Al Jazeera reports, with the price of flour, eggs, onions and other staples rising sharply since Wednesday, when Israel said commercial goods would no longer enter. The closure is linked to a dispute over fees involving Palestinian merchants and Hamas. A resident of Jabalia told Al Jazeera a carton of eggs that cost 35 shekels ($11.34) is now selling for more, and that closures have become a recurring cycle followed by price spikes. A funeral was held for 75 Palestinians whose remains were recovered from the ruins in Gaza City, most from the Daraj neighbourhood, according to the Health Ministry.

In Caracas, the opposition's Unitary Democratic Platform (PUD) reaffirmed Maria Corina Machado as its leader at a meeting on Sunday and issued 14 proposals for a democratic transition — free parties, release of political prisoners, safe return of exiles, and new elections. Machado, the exiled Nobel laureate, has petitioned for new elections and for permission to return. Venezuela has not set a date for a presidential vote and has been led since January 3 by interim President Delcy Rodriguez of the PSUV. Former presidential candidate Edmundo Gonzalez endorsed the platform on X.

The Gaza closure is a leverage move by Israel against Hamas's fee collection; the Venezuela statement is a test of whether a fractured opposition can hold together long enough to force an election calendar. Neither is a new war, but both constrain what the US can claim to have stabilised.
sections.whyItMatters: Gaza's food prices are the most sensitive indicator of whether the ceasefire framework holds through winter. Machado's consolidation matters because Washington's Venezuela policy has no other viable interlocutor.

bottomLine: The day's defining fact is that Ukraine can still hit Russia hard — 1,015 drones, a burning oil terminal outside St Petersburg, an airport closed — while its principal backer argues publicly against the method and has paused sanctions on the target. That is an alliance problem, not a battlefield one. Simultaneously, Beijing is expanding its below-threshold squeeze on Taiwan with 16 vessels in a single coordinated sweep, France is convulsing over the cost of living with 2,400 arrests and a burned city hall, and the EU is quietly restricting the steel exports Ukraine needs to keep fighting. The common thread is not a single crisis but the erosion of the political margin in allied capitals: Washington's patience with Kyiv, Brussels' appetite for Ukrainian exports, and Paris' capacity to govern are all shrinking at once, while Moscow, Beijing and Tehran keep testing where the limits are.
